newsitem.title: FRANCE: NATO-Russia deal may not be ready for Paris summit.
newsitem.headline: NATO-Russia deal may not be ready for Paris summit.

text.p: Talks between NATO and Russia on establishing a new relationship were heading in the right direction but might not be over in time for a planned signing in Paris on May 27, NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana said on Wednesday.
"I think the discussions are going in the right direction but I don't know if we will make it in time," Solana said after meeting French Prime Minister Alain Juppe.
"I hope we will and we will work intensely to do it."
Solana later met French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette who acknowledged negotiations were difficult but he voiced hopes that an agreement could be reached within weeks.
"I believe the coming weeks will allow us to finalise this exercise," he told reporters.
The French Foreign Ministry said earlier that the May 27 Paris summit would only take place if an agreement had been reached.

Agreement would set the stage for a July North Atlantic Treaty Organisation summit in Madrid at which the defence alliance is expected to invite several former Communist Warsaw Pact countries to start negotiations on full membership.
The first wave of nations asked to join the alliance's eastward expansion is expected to be made up of Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.
Solana and Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov failed to iron out differences in talks in Moscow on Tuesday, and substantial issues remain ahead of the July summit.
"In all our meetings we make progress. Yesterday, too, we made progress, but problems remain to be overcome," Solana said in Paris.

Russia, which has conceded that it cannot stop the expansion, has sought to win an agreement that NATO will not permanently station troops or build permanent bases on the territory of new central European member states.
The United States has stressed it will not accept any deal that gives candidate states second-class status.

Solana was hopeful that France and the United States would reach in the near term a satisfactory agreement on Paris' demand that NATO's U.S.-held southern command be transferred to a European officer.
"NATO is an organisation that knows very well how to find consensus," he said. "I believe it will find a solution that France can be comfortable with."
He said his talks with de Charette only covered negotiations with Russia and did not touch on the dispute between Paris and Washington.
The planned Paris summit has raised expectations that Chirac might accept a compromise on the issue of the Naples command.
France has tied the issue to its decision to re-join the military wing of a reformed NATO alliance.
